ADDICTION TREATMENT

While making substance abuse treatment available to individuals with opioid analgesic dependence is one of the
recommendations being made by officials from the CDC and ONDCP, so far
there is a very limited evidence base to
guide treatment in this population. However, a new study provides evidence that
longer-term medical treatment and counseling are likely necessary.
Most research on the treatment of
opioid-dependent individuals has focused on individuals addicted to heroin
who are treated in methadone clinics,
but there are key differences between

heroin users and prescription opioid
abusers that may affect treatment outcomes. For example, individuals who
abuse prescription opioids are less likely
to have ever injected drugs, are more
likely to be employed and have family
support, and are likely to have used an
opioid for a shorter period on average
than heroin users. This has led some to
suggest that these prescription opioid
abusers may be easier to treat. However, the first large randomized controlled trial of medical treatment and
counseling for prescription analgesic
abusers suggests that such individuals
are likely to be similar to those who use
heroin.
Roger D. Weiss, MD, of Harvard MedicalSchoolandtheDivisionofAlcoholand
Drug Abuse at McLean Hospital in Belmont, Mass, and his colleagues randomized653individualswhoweredependent
onprescriptionopioidsto2weeksoftreatment with buprenorphine-naloxone followed by a 2-week taper and 8 weeks of
postmedication follow-up; half of the patients also received opioid dependence
counseling (Weiss RD et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry. doi:10.1001/archgenpsychiatry
.2011.121 [published online November
7, 2011]). Patients who successfully
ended opioid use after this brief treatment left the trial; those who did not were
then enrolled in an extended 12-week

program and randomized to receive treatment with buprenorphine-naloxone,
with or without counseling, followed by
a 4-week taper and 8 weeks of postmedication follow-up.
Only 6.6% patients were successful
after the brief treatment, regardless of
whether they received counseling.
About half of the patients were successful in their attempts to stop opioid
medication abuse during the 12-week
treatment period, again regardless of
whether they received counseling. But
successful abstinence was short-lived
for many patients, with only 8.6%
remaining abstinent 8 weeks after the
end of the 4-week buprenorphinenaloxone taper period.
Weiss said in an interview that the
results are consistent with studies of
heroin use treatment. “Detoxification
is not very effective,” he said, adding
that longer-term treatment with medications, primarily methadone maintenance, has been shown to be more effective than detoxification for patients
with heroin addiction. He noted that
further research on the use of buprenorphine to treat opioid dependence and
on the prescription opioid–abusing
population is needed.
“[Clinicians] should strongly consider ongoing pharmacotherapy with
this population,” he said. 䊐

Researchers Still Seek Clinical Benefit
in Raising Levels of Good Cholesterol
Mike Mitka
O RLANDO , F LA —The use of statin
therapy to lower levels of low-density
lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C),
the “bad cholesterol,” is one of the pillars of cardiovascular disease prevention. But even individuals who have low
LDL-C levels can die from cardiovascular disease, leaving researchers to
question whether other changes to a patient’s lipid profile might reduce that
risk.

A hypothesis that is embraced by
many in the medical community involves high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), the “good cholesterol.” Epidemiologic studies have
found an inverse association between
HDL-C levels and the rates of coronary heart disease events, so researchers theorize that raising HDL-C levels
might reduce adverse coronary outcomes. However, proof of the theory remains outside researchers’ grasp, as
shown in studies presented at the

Recent research on drugs to raise
HDL-C levels has centered on
extended-release niacin and cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP)
inhibition. Niacin has been shown to
increase HDL-C by up to 35% and
reduce all-cause mortality; however,
niacin also lowers LDL-C and triglycerides, which confounds the significance of its effect on HDL-C. CETP
inhibitors increase HDL-C levels and

At the meeting, results from the
Atherothrombosis Intervention in
Metabolic Syndrome with Low HDL/
High Triglycerides: Impact on Global
Health Outcomes (AIM-HIGH) trial
cast doubt on niacin’s therapeutic
potential. The AIM-HIGH investigators randomized 3414 patients to
receive simvastatin plus extendedrelease niacin (1500 mg to 2000 mg
daily) or placebo (which included a
low [50-mg] dose of niacin, to cause
flushing, to maintain blinding).
At 2 years, patients receiving niacin
plus simvastatin experienced a significant increase in HDL-C levels, from 35
mg/dL to 42 mg/dL, and a reduction in
LDL-C levels, from 74 mg/dL to 62
mg/dL; in those who received placebo
plus simvastatin, HDL-C levels
increased from 35 mg/dL to 38 mg/dL
and LDL-C levels decreased from 74
mg/dL to 67 mg/dL. But there was no
difference between the 2 groups in
occurrence of the primary end point,
which was the first event of death
from coronary heart disease, nonfatal myocardial infarction, ischemic
stroke, hospitalization for an acute
coronary syndrome, or symptomdriven coronary or cerebral revascularization. The trial was stopped
early due to a lack of efficacy (Boden
WE et al. N Engl J Med. doi:10.1056
/NEJMoa1107579 [published online
November 15, 2011]).
William Boden, MD, AIM-HIGH
co–principal investigator and professor of medicine at the University of
Buffalo in New York, was surprised by
the result. “Why did the drug do
everything you expected it to do and
yet not reduce events?” Boden said.
“If you look at the clinical trial landscape, it’s littered with attempts to
raise HDL-C and reduce events. We
have solid epidemiologic evidence
that low levels of HDL-C are associated with residual risk, but we have
yet to demonstrate therapeutic benefits from treatments.”

Phillip Barter, MD, PhD, the discussant of the AIM-HIGH trial and a professor of medicine at the University of
Sydney in Australia, strongly disagreed with Boden’s conclusions.
“This trial disturbs me greatly,” said
Barter who added. “It disturbs me
because the design was such that in
no way could it test the hypothesis of

its HDL-C levels increase (perhaps
due to the use of the small dose of
niacin), which could perhaps explain
the lack of efficacy found in the treatment group.
Allen J. Taylor, MD, director of advanced cardiovascular imaging and the
lipid clinic at Washington Hospital Center in Washington, DC, sided with Barter’s arguments.
“My feeling is that this trial’s design
was a severely confounded attempt to
understand how niacin would add to
statin therapy, making the results become almost meaningless,” Taylor said.
“I think it would be a mistake for any
clinician to change what they are doing treating their patients based on the
AIM-HIGH results.”
Boden said that while some may criticize the AIM-HIGH trial design, it does
add to the current understanding of

with stable nonacute cardiovascular
disease and LDL-C levels that were
achieved and maintained below 70 mg/
dL, we could find or demonstrate no incremental clinical benefit from the addition of niacin to statin therapy during
a 36-month follow-up despite significant improvements in both HDL-C and
triglycerides,” Boden said.
While the AIM-HIGH results were
questioned, another study that examined the effects of a CETP inhibitor was
welcomed. In a randomized trial involving 398 patients followed up for 12
weeks, researchers found that the CETP
inhibitor evacetrapib, used either alone
or in combination with statins, raised
HDL-C levels and lowered LDL-C levels compared with placebo or statin
monotherapy (Nicholls SJ et al. JAMA.
2011;306[19]:2099-2109).
Evacetrapib joins dalcetrapib and anacetrapib as CETP inhibitors that have
successfully raised HDL-C levels with
no observed safety risks. The safety profile of these drugs will be followed
closely because the phase 3 trial of the
first CETP inhibitor, torcetrapib, was
stopped early in 2006 due to an unexpected increase in all-cause mortality
that was believed to have been caused
by off-target effects.
“This is an exciting class of drugs,
and there is considerable hope that this
may well be the next big thing to put
on top of a statin. We now have to show
if evacetrapib reduces morbidity and
mortality in a big phase 3 trial, and
when that happens has yet to be determined,” said Stephen J. Nicholls, MBBS,
PhD, lead researcher and cardiovascular director of the Cleveland Clinic Coordinating Center for Clinical Research in Ohio.
As for whether these CETP inhibitors are successful, Boden cautions that
optimism might need to be guarded. “In
the era of aggressive statin therapy
where you can get patients treated to a
low LDL-C, is there incremental benefit to raising residual levels of HDL-C?
If you can achieve and maintain low
levels of LDL-C, HDL-C may not be a
worthy target,” said Boden. 䊐
